name: Attentional Bias
description: A person's attention is pulled disproportionately toward certain kinds of stimuli rather than distributed evenly across what is present. In practice this usually means emotionally charged, threatening, craving-related, or goal-relevant cues get noticed first and held longer.
design_relevance_note: Most relevant in health, safety, finance, and behavior-change products where threat, craving, or emotionally loaded cues can dominate attention; much less a general-purpose interface law than selective-attention limits or banner blindness.
myth_risk_note: Well-established via meta-analysis for threat-related attentional bias specifically; broader non-emotional applications of the term are supported by separate, not-yet-unified literatures, so the popular general-purpose label is broader than any single meta-analytic finding covers. Re-checked 2026-09-09 (Round 11): confirmed this entry's own topic rests entirely on Bar-Haim et al.'s (2007) meta-analysis of 172 studies (N=4,031) -- genuinely fine, not a single-study-risk gap, the same 'one source that is itself a meta-analysis' pattern as Scarcity Principle. No promotion needed.
prevalence_note: A standard term in psychology and behavior-change work, and sometimes relevant in safety/addiction-adjacent UX, but not a mainstream named law in day-to-day product-design canon.

findings.description: A meta-analytic review found reliable threat-related attentional bias in anxious relative to nonanxious individuals across established attention paradigms, directly backing the narrower clinical/emotional core of 'attentional bias' rather than every broader use of the label.
findings.source_title: Threat-related attentional bias in anxious and nonanxious individuals: A meta-analytic study.
